input:
In this example we consider a blackened plate that is held at a temperature of 600 K and faces surroundings that are at a temperature of 290 K, with the emissivity of the plate being 0.9. The quantity that we wish to determine is the net radiative heat flux, denoted $q$, and the relevant relation is the Stefan-Boltzmann expression

$$q = \varepsilon \sigma (T_1^4 - T_2^4)$$

in which $T_1$ is the temperature of the plate, $T_2$ is the temperature of the surroundings, $\varepsilon$ is the emissivity, and $\sigma$ is the Stefan-Boltzmann constant, which has the value 5.67 x 10-8 W m-2 K-4. When the stated values are substituted into this expression, the net radiative heat flux is found to be 6.3 kW m-2, which represents the net rate at which energy is exchanged per unit area once the radiation received from the surroundings has been set against the radiation emitted by the plate itself.

It should be noted, however, that this estimate rests on the assumption that both surfaces are large and parallel to one another. View factors for the real geometry are not included in the calculation, so the result should be understood as applying to the idealised arrangement described by the equation rather than to any actual arrangement in which the plate is of finite size or the surroundings only partially enclose it.
target:
A blackened plate at temperature $T_1$ = 600 K faces surroundings at $T_2$ = 290 K. The emissivity $\varepsilon$ of the plate is 0.9. The net radiative heat flux $q$ from the plate is given by

$$q = \varepsilon \sigma (T_1^4 - T_2^4)$$

where $\sigma$ is the Stefan-Boltzmann constant. The flux is the difference of two fourth-power terms: the plate emits on its own temperature and receives on the temperature of the surroundings, and the emissivity scales the exchange below the blackbody value at the same temperatures. The net flux is the difference between the radiation the plate sends out and the radiation it receives back from the surroundings. Each side of the difference is set by the temperature of the surface it leaves, raised to the fourth power, so the hotter side dominates the balance and the exchange runs outward from the plate, from the hot surface toward the cold surroundings, at every point the two face each other. With $\sigma$ = 5.67 x 10-8 W m-2 K-4, substitution of the stated temperatures and emissivity gives $q$ = 6.3 kW m-2.

The estimate treats both surfaces as large and parallel. View factors for the real geometry are not included, so the value holds for the idealised arrangement the equation describes; a plate of finite size, or surroundings that enclose it only in part, exchange on view factors this estimate does not carry, and the flux for such a geometry is not the figure computed here.
